Project task 15.3 – Cleaning up
In this project task, you will terminate the EC2 instance by deleting the CloudFormation stack.
You should not manually terminate resources deployed by CloudFormation as this causes a
configuration drift with the stack. Always delete the stack in CloudFormation, and the service
will delete any resources that belong to the stack. You can also define deletion policies to retain
any resources you might need after stack deletions, such as a backup of a database.
Navigate back to the AWS CloudFormation console
From the left-hand menu, click on Stacks
In the right-hand pane, select your stack
Click the Delete stack button
In the pop-up window that appears, type in the name of your stack in the text box and
click the Delete stack button
Your stack will now be deleted, and any resources created, such as the EC2 instance, will be
terminated.

4.5 447 Automation, Deployment, and Additional AWS Services
Summary
In this chapter, you discovered how businesses want to be able to focus on their application
design and development rather than the underlying heavy lifting associated with
infrastructure provisioning, deployment, and management. Companies do not want to spend
hours maintaining and managing their infrastructure and instead need to focus on building
new features and resolving bugs within their applications.
Furthermore, the ability to automate infrastructure provisioning and management in a
repeatable and consistent manner is critical to avoid potential discrepancies in minute
configuration items of those resources, which often lead to confusion and delayed
troubleshooting exercises.
To help customers automate and manage their infrastructure resources efficiently, AWS offers
PaaS tools such as Elastic Beanstalk and IaC solutions such as CloudFormation.
AWS Elastic Beanstalk is designed to help developers focus on their code. Developers can
upload their code in a supported language and framework and have Elastic Beanstalk
provision all the necessary infrastructure resources to host the application.
AWS CloudFormation is an IaC platform, enabling you to define your infrastructure resources
using YAML or JSON templates. You can create templates that define complete end-to-end
architecture patterns and deploy the required resources as stacks fully managed by the
CloudFormation service.
Finally, you learned about various developer tools that support your application and software
development lifecycle (SDLC) process using CI/CD services such as AWS CodeCommit,
CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, and CodePipeline.
In the next chapter, you will learn about monitoring and managing your resources on AWS.
While architecting, building, and deploying solutions play an important role as a Cloud
Practitioner, supporting existing environments, managing, and maintaining workloads so that
they operate at optimal levels is just as critical. The chapter introduces you to tools that help
you analyze the health and performance of your resources and take appropriate actions to
ensure reliability and stability. You will also learn how to audit access and enforce governance
while also understanding concepts related to change management. In addition, you will learn
about various tools to help you efficiently manage fleets of resources.

Chapter 15 450
16
Management and Governance on
AWS
As a cloud practitioner, you must ensure that the wide range of resources you provision to host
your application are highly available, secure, and perform as expected. You must continuously
monitor your underlying resources and identify any potential performance issues that could
cause bottlenecks. These issues should be addressed at the earliest and, with the help of
monitoring and logging solutions available on AWS, even prevented.
You must also be able to audit your environment to ensure that you prevent any unauthorized
access or deployments and detect anomalies that may indicate performance or security issues.
Furthermore, you must enforce proper change management processes to ensure that all
changes made to resources are compliant with organizational requirements and to prevent
unauthorized changes.
Finally, as part of your day-to-day management, you must also be able to effectively manage
your resources—such as patching, performing updates, and automating maintenance tasks.
In this chapter, you will look at a series of AWS services that enable you to effectively monitor
and manage your AWS resources. You can use these services to ensure your resources operate
efficiently and within acceptable performance standards. You can also audit and log all
requests made in your AWS account to ensure you have a trail of all activities, enabling you to
stay compliant. Finally, you can enforce rules to ensure resources provisioned, or changes made
to existing ones, are in accordance with business goals and objectives.
The following topics are covered in this chapter:
Observing workloads with Amazon CloudWatch
Meeting compliance requirements with AWS CloudTrail
Managing change control with AWS Config
Automating resource administration with AWS Systems Manager
Improving workloads with AWS Trusted Advisor
Observing workloads with Amazon CloudWatch
Amazon CloudWatch is a fully idx_2c9b9c0d managed monitoring and logging service designed to help you
monitor and analyze the health of your AWS resources and applications. With Amazon
CloudWatch, you can see how your resources are performing in real time. You can collect
measurements (called metrics) from your idx_b40742cd resources hosted on AWS as well as from on-
premises locations.
A metric represents a time-ordered set of data points that are published to CloudWatch. An
example of a metric is CPU Utilization for an EC2 instance, expressed as a percentage over time.
If a particular instance is consuming more than 95% CPU utilization for an extended period,
you may wish to investigate it, as this could affect performance for your end users.
You can also use Amazon CloudWatch to collect application log data as key-value pairs, which
can be used to identify issues with applications such as errors, timeouts, and more. Thus, in

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 15 450
chunks.content:
addition to capturing metric data from resources such as EC2 instances, RDS databases, and
DynamoDB tables, you can also obtain logging information for applications, such as Apache
web servers, Nginx, WordPress, and more.
Some typical use cases for Amazon CloudWatch include the following:
Infrastructure monitoring and troubleshooting: Monitor resource metrics and logs
and visualize trends over time to identify potential bottlenecks. This can be used to
conduct root cause analysis to resolve incidents and problems.
Proactive resource optimization: Configure alarms that monitor metric values and
are triggered when defined thresholds are crossed for a specified period. You can also
define automated remediation actions, such as configuring Auto Scaling to launch
additional resources to distribute load or restarting or terminating instances.

chunks.heading: Chapter 16 452
chunks.content:
Chapter 16 452
Log analytics: Analyze log files from a wide range of application sources to identify
operational issues, bugs, and potential security exploits, as well as to determine
application performance and health.
In the next section, you idx_4546fa34 will learn more about how Amazon CloudWatch organizes and
categorizes metrics data so that it is easy to consume and analyze.
CloudWatch namespaces, dimensions, and metrics
Before using Amazon idx_f3196431 CloudWatch, it idx_92bec069 is important to idx_5aefd2a5 understand how the service captures
metric and log data and how it categorizes this data. Amazon CloudWatch uses the concepts of
namespaces, dimensions, and metrics. Let's look at them in a bit more detail:
CloudWatch namespaces: A namespace is a logical container idx_ee917dca used to group metric
data that belongs to a specific AWS service. The screenshot depicted in Figure 16.1
showcases a few common namespaces. So, for example, you have a namespace called
AWS/EC2 to capture idx_bd73056c all metrics related to your EC2 instances.
Figure 16.1: CloudWatch metrics namespaces
In addition to the standard namespaces defined by AWS, you can create custom
namespaces to idx_66e80ddb capture custom metrics, such as those idx_9b2dcdb0 related to idx_6fe9c2ad third-party
applications running on your EC2 instances.
CloudWatch dimensions: Dimensions represent the individual resource that you are
monitoring. For example, dimensions related to your EC2 instances include the
individual instance ID whose metrics you are monitoring, as depicted in Figure 16.2:
•
•
•
453 Management and Governance on AWS
Figure 16.2: Individual instances represent the dimensions of the EC2 namespace
CloudWatch metrics: These are the individual measurements for the resource you are
monitoring, such idx_fd4505c6 as CPU idx_bc957bb2 Utilization, Network idx_54aafb78 Bytes In/Out, Disk Read/Write, and
more.
In the next section, you will explore CloudWatch metrics in greater depth.
More on CloudWatch metrics
Amazon CloudWatch idx_e96b508b metrics are time-ordered sets of data points. Resources that you
provision on AWS will report a wide range of standard metrics to CloudWatch by default. For
example, you could monitor the CPU Utilization metric consumed by a specific EC2 instance as
a percentage over a period. This can help you track performance trends, identify spikes, and
determine if the resource is being overutilized.
Figure 16.3 depicts the CPU Utilization of an EC2 instance running in the us-east-1 region. This
instance is a t3.micro instance (it has 1 vCPU and 1 GB RAM).
Figure 16.3: CPU utilization for a t3.micro instance over a 12-hour period
Using the data points captured, you can identify any bottlenecks or potential issues over time.
•

chunks.heading: Chapter 16 454
chunks.content:
Chapter 16 454
Amazon CloudWatch offers a wide range of built-in metrics across its vast array of services and
resources. However, you may also need to collect custom metrics, as discussed next:
Built-in metrics: Amazon CloudWatch allows you to collect a wide range of default
metrics. These metrics are captured from the underlying infrastructure, such as the
host machines and the hypervisor layer. An example of this is CPU utilization, which
captures how much CPU is being consumed from the allocated capacity at the
hypervisor level. Other examples include disk read/write and data transfer metrics.
Custom metrics: If you need to capture operating system-level or application-level
metrics, you must install a CloudWatch agent on the resource, such as an EC2 instance.
Examples include web application load times, request error rates, and more. Another
example of a custom metric is operating system memory consumption. This is because,
unlike CPU utilization, which monitors underlying hardware CPU usage patterns,
memory metrics operate at the OS level and are not monitored by default.
While capturing all these idx_a1f0e6ea different metrics over a period is useful, the ability to present the
data in an easily digestible form is crucial for quickly identifying trends and issues. Amazon
CloudWatch offers the ability to create custom dashboards, which are discussed next.
CloudWatch dashboards
Amazon CloudWatch idx_7f13bb40 offers a dashboard feature enabling you to present captured metrics and
logging data that offer visualization capabilities through charts and graphs.
You can use CloudWatch dashboards to provide insights into your resources' health across
AWS accounts and regions using the cross-account functionality and integrate this with AWS
organizations. This enables you to create cross-account dashboards.
An example of how you can represent your captured metrics data using dashboards is depicted
in Figure 16.4:
Figure 16.4: Amazon CloudWatch dashboards
•
•
455 Management and Governance on AWS
In addition to monitoring your resources using CloudWatch dashboards, you can also create
alarms that trigger when idx_40ea7fe9 specified threshold values are breached. This is discussed in the next
section.
CloudWatch alarms
You can idx_89f7fca5 configure CloudWatch alarms to monitor idx_46df14fd a given resource's metrics, for example, the
average CPU utilization of an EC2 instance. If the metric crosses a specific threshold value that
you define, it can trigger an alarm. Note that the alarm will only trigger once the threshold
value is breached for more than a defined period. This helps prevent false positives caused by
momentary spikes.
For example, you may wish to trigger an alarm if the CPU utilization on an EC2 instance is over
90% for more than 15 minutes.

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 16 454
chunks.content:
CloudWatch alarms can be in any one of three states:
OK: Occurs when the idx_c830b23f metric is within the range defined as acceptable
Alarm: Occurs when the metric is outside the specified range. This can be either above
or below the defined threshold
Insufficient data: Occurs when the data needed to determine the alarm state is
missing or idx_a52ec6a4 incomplete. Typically, an alarm is in this state when it is first created, while
it begins collecting metric data
Once an alarm has been triggered, you can automate certain actions to be taken in response.
These include:
Simple Notification Service (SNS) notification: You can send an automatic
notification to idx_f28f8993 an administrator or push the notification to an application or a Lambda
function to perform an automated remediation task
Auto Scaling action: For EC2 instances, you can trigger an Auto Scaling action when
the alarm is triggered to launch or terminate instances as required, ensuring that the
metric falls back within acceptable ranges
EC2 action: You can configure an alarm to trigger an EC2 instance action, such as
stopping or restarting the instance. For certain instance types, you can also perform an
instance recovery, which means the instance is relaunched on different host hardware.
This is particularly useful if the underlying hardware on which the EC2 instance was
originally running is experiencing an issue
You can also publish your idx_2159241a alarms to CloudWatch dashboards, giving you instant visibility
when alarms are triggered.
•
•
•
•
•
•

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 16 456
chunks.content:
Chapter 16 456
In addition to metrics, CloudWatch allows you to ingest logging data across both AWS services
and third-party applications. CloudWatch Logs is discussed in the next section.
CloudWatch logs
Amazon CloudWatch idx_ac867e28 also offers the ability to capture logging data across a wide range of AWS
services, as well as third-party applications that you host on Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon
ECS clusters, and AWS Lambda functions. For example, you can ingest VPC Flow Logs into
CloudWatch Logs, which allows you to analyze network traffic flowing into and out of your
VPCs. You can also capture logs from services such as AWS CloudTrail, Amazon Route 53, and
many more. Examples of third-party application logs that you can capture include web server
access logs, error logs, and operating system event logs.
You can ingest logs regardless of their source, and they are stored as a series of time-ordered
events that you can query, analyze, search, and filter for specific patterns or error codes. You
can also visually analyze your logging data using CloudWatch dashboards.
Logging data can be retained indefinitely for historical analysis, although many organizations
configure retention periods ranging from 1 day to 10 years to meet compliance requirements.
You can also archive your logging data to Amazon S3 buckets and use one of the Amazon S3
Glacier storage classes to keep costs to a minimum.
In the next section, you will learn idx_94309819 about another management and governance service known
as AWS CloudTrail. This service is designed to help you audit access patterns and enforce
governance and compliance.
Meeting compliance requirements with AWS
CloudTrail
As part of your overall idx_0fc50997 management, governance, and security toolkit, you must monitor access
patterns and track all actions that take place in your AWS account – be they provisioning or
terminating resources, or even as simple as an IAM user logging into your AWS account, having
read access to those resources and applications. Amazon CloudTrail is an auditing service that
records every single API call made to your AWS account and the resources contained within.
Amazon CloudTrail is enabled by default and records all activities you perform in your AWS
account. For example, if a user Alice logs in to the account and launches an EC2 instance, and
then later terminates it, all these individual actions are recorded as depicted in the following
screenshot in Figure 16.5.
457 Management and Governance on AWS
Figure 16.5: Amazon CloudTrail event history
With Amazon CloudTrail, you can monitor and enforce compliance and governance by
responding to the idx_a11767cc recorded time-ordered series of events that take place in your AWS
account. You can ingest these events into Amazon CloudWatch and Amazon EventBridge to

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 16 456
chunks.content:
trigger automated remediation actions, such as invoking AWS Lambda functions or sending
alert notifications using Amazon SNS.
Amazon CloudTrail provides a history of both API and non-API activities. API activities
include actions such as launching an EC2 instance or deleting an Amazon S3 bucket. Non-API
activities include actions such as logging in to the AWS Management Console.
Amazon CloudTrail allows you to record the following types of events:
Management events: These provide idx_db0a2cb3 information about management operations that
you perform in your AWS account. Also known as control plane operations, examples
include API calls such as the RunInstances operation when you launch a new EC2
instance. Management events include both write-only and read-only events.
For example, when Alice launches an EC2 instance (as shown in Figure 16.5), she
performs a write-only event. A read-only event would include an API operation such as
DescribeInstances, which returns a list of EC2 instances without making any
changes. Management events can also include non-API activities, such as when a user
logs in to the AWS Management Console.
Data events: These provide information about operations performed on or within a
resource in your AWS account. For example, when you upload an object to an Amazon
S3 bucket, you perform the PutObject API operation. Another example of a data event
is adding items to a DynamoDB table, which results in a PutItem API operation.
•
•

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 16 458
chunks.content:
Chapter 16 458
Data events are idx_dd5d52ef known as data plane operations and are generally high volume. Data
events are not logged by default, and you must explicitly configure a trail and specify
the supported resources or resource types for which you want to collect these events.
Insight events: These provide details about unusual activities in your AWS account.
You must idx_2efea8ca enable Insight events to allow CloudTrail to detect such behavior. For
example, if your account normally logs one or two Amazon S3 DeleteBucket API calls
per minute, but suddenly starts logging 200 DeleteBucket calls per minute, this may
be recorded as unusual activity.
Amazon CloudTrail Events idx_ab334d38 stores all management events for up to 90 days, which you can view
in the console or download. Furthermore, the event history will not provide any information
on data events—for these, you must create a trail, which is discussed in the next section.
Regional and global trails
If you need to store data idx_3a5f40dc events or management events beyond the default 90-day retention
period, you must create a specific Amazon CloudTrail trail. A trail is a configuration that
enables CloudTrail to record specific types of events and store them in Amazon S3 and
optionally in AWS CloudWatch Logs.
Trails can be configured to record events from a single region or across all regions:
All-Regions trail: CloudTrail records events in each AWS region and delivers them as
log files to the Amazon S3 bucket that you specify. When you configure CloudTrail to
record events from all regions, any new regions launched by AWS are automatically
included. The All-Regions trail is also the default option when you create a trail using
the CloudTrail console.
Single-Region trail: In some cases, you may only require trail data from a specific
region. You can configure a trail to record log files and event data from a single region
and have them delivered to an Amazon S3 bucket of your choice.
You can also idx_bc09fde2 create an AWS Organization trail, which records events from the management
account as well as all member accounts in the AWS Organizations environment. This approach
ensures that you record important management events across all member accounts,
supporting centralized auditing, and compliance requirements.
In the next section, you will learn about another service that allows you to analyze and
evaluate changes to your idx_629324d4 resources over a period. This is particularly useful when you want to
enforce change management processes and ensure that any configuration you implement is in
alignment with corporate governance and rules.
•
•
•
459 Management and Governance on AWS
Managing change control with AWS Config
AWS Config is a service idx_3a1e37d1 that enables you to monitor how your resources are configured and

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 16 458
chunks.content:
track changes to those configurations over time. You can also gain insights into how those
resources were configured in the past, including resources that have since been deleted.
In addition, you can define rules to ensure that any resources created are compliant with
predefined configurations. For example, you may wish to enforce a rule that all Amazon S3
buckets have versioning enabled. If versioning has not been set, AWS Config will flag the
bucket as non-compliant.
With AWS Config, you can monitor changes to individual configuration items of your
resources. A configuration item is a point-in-time snapshot of the attributes for a given
resource in your AWS account. A configuration item includes information such as metadata,
attributes, relationships with other resources, and the resource's current configuration.
For example, when you deploy an EC2 instance, one configuration item is the instance type. If
you select the t3.micro instance type, that value represents a configuration item for the EC2
instance being deployed.
When you make changes to a resource, you modify its configuration items—for example, when
you upgrade an idx_418b61be instance type from t3.micro to t3.small. This change is recorded in a JSON
diff file, highlighting the fields that have changed, as shown in Figure 16.6:
Figure 16.6: AWS Config monitoring changes to resource config

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 16 460
chunks.content:
Chapter 16 460
AWS Config can also help businesses manage their change management workflows by
providing evidence of configuration changes, which can be used for troubleshooting purposes.
So far, you have learned about various tools that help you monitor resources, capture metrics
and logging data, audit activity, and document resource changes, as well as enforce resource
configurations using rules. As part of the management and governance toolkit, you also need
mechanisms to automate management tasks across your resources, such as patching EC2
instances, implementing automation workflows, and administering your environments. In the
next section, you idx_949fc1ff will learn about AWS Systems Manager, which offers a wide range of tools to
help you efficiently manage and administer your AWS resources.
Automating resource administration with AWS
Systems Manager
AWS Systems Manager is a suite idx_b65a4714 of services that enables you to centrally manage and
administer your AWS resources. With AWS Systems Manager, you gain visibility into the
resources provisioned in your AWS account, as well as the ability to automate and perform
day-to-day operational tasks.
AWS Systems Manager uses the concept of documents, which are written in JSON or YAML
format and define the actions to be taken against those resources. AWS offers a wide range of
predefined documents, or you can create your own. For example, the AWS-
ArchiveEBSVolumeSnapshots document can be used to identify EBS snapshots that match a
specific tag key and value, evaluate them against a defined retention policy, and then archive
them to reduce storage costs. A screenshot is presented in Figure 16.7:
Figure 16.7: AWS Systems Manager documents
461 Management and Governance on AWS
AWS Systems Manager offers a wide range of tools and services to enable your operations team
to centrally and idx_b59ba2d9 efficiently manage all resources deployed in your AWS account. These include:
Run Command: The Run Command is a feature that enables you to remotely run Linux
shell scripts and Windows PowerShell commands across your fleet of EC2 instances.
This allows you to deploy configuration changes or install and update applications
across multiple instances in one shot, without individually connecting to each
instance.
State Manager: This offers the ability to design and maintain consistent
configurations across your EC2 instances, such as firewall settings, antivirus
configurations, and more.
Inventory: This service enables you to capture software configuration information
about your EC2 instances. These include details about how the operating system
configuration, including DHCP settings, agent details, and any custom items. You can
run queries to track and audit your systems.
Maintenance Window: Part of the change management capability, the Maintenance

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 16 460
chunks.content:
Window service enables you to schedule times when administrative tasks, such as
installing patches, can be performed.
Patch Manager: This service enables you to automate patch deployments to your EC2
instances. You can obtain information on which patches have been deployed and
which patches are pending across both operating systems and application patches.
Parameter Store: This service enables you to store sensitive information such as
database endpoints, usernames and passwords, API keys, and other configuration
details in an encrypted store. Application running on your instances can reference
these configuration details by making API calls to Parameter Store when required. This
ensures that you do not need to hardcode sensitive data in application code or store it
on instances in plain text.
Session Manager: This service enables you to remotely access your Linux and
Windows-based instances using a browser-based interactive shell and CLI. The service
uses standard HTTPS (port 443) to connect you to the shell interface of your instance,
meaning that you do not need to open unnecessary ports for remote administration.
This also means you do not need to provision Bastion Hosts in public subnets, which
can increase security risks.
AWS Systems Manager has several additional tools to help you efficiently manage your
resources, such idx_32751756 as your EC2 instances in your AWS account. In the next section, you will learn
about the AWS Trusted Advisor service, which enables you to inspect your AWS environment
and identify whether your resources have been configured in accordance with best practices.
•

chunks.heading: Chapter 16 462
chunks.content:
Chapter 16 462
Improving workloads with AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS Trusted Advisor is a service idx_dd562b5a that enables you to analyze your workloads and how they
are configured against AWS-recommended best practices across five different categories.
These best practices help you identify opportunities to improve resource performance,
reliability, security, and cost-effectiveness. AWS Trusted Advisor uses a color-coded system to
highlight key configuration findings, as follows:
Green: Trusted Advisor has not identified any issues, and your resources comply with
best practices
Yellow: Trusted Advisor detects a potential issue and recommends reviewing your
configuration. For example, if you are consuming more than 80% of a particular service
limit, this will be highlighted
Red: Trusted Advisor recommends that you take immediate action to resolve critical
issues. For example, if you have opened port 3389 (RDP) to allow access to a Windows
EC2 instance from the entire internet (0.0.0.0/0), this is considered a security risk
The five categories used idx_0bc50812 to guide how your resources should be configured are:
Performance: Provides recommendations on how you can modify your existing
infrastructure architecture and configurations to improve performance. This category
helps identify over-utilized resources and recommends upgrades where appropriate
Security: Reports on resources that are not configured in accordance with security best
practices. For example, if multi-factor authentication (MFA) is not enabled on the
root user idx_5b28085f account, AWS highlights this as a critical security risk.
Fault tolerance: Identifies resources that should be reconfigured to improve resilience
and reduce single points of failure
Cost optimization: Performs checks to identify opportunities to reduce costs and
avoid waste. This may include recommendations such as moving from On-Demand
pricing to Reserved Instances or using appropriate Savings Plans
Service limits: Checks whether your AWS resources are approaching service limits or
quotas and alerts you accordingly
AWS Trusted Advisor is a go-to tool for obtaining a detailed breakdown of how your AWS
resources are configured and for analyzing recommendations to align them with industry best
practices and AWS guidance.
It is important to note that AWS Trusted Advisor is not entirely free. The available checks and
reporting features depend on the AWS Support plan you have subscribed to. With the Basic
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
463 Management and Governance on AWS
Support plan, you only have access to a limited set of core checks. To gain access to the full
range of recommendations across all five categories, you must subscribe to at least the
Business Support plan.
In the next idx_7fb5bd0b section, you will carry out a project task to monitor a resource using Amazon

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 16 462
chunks.content:
CloudWatch and configure alarms.

Summary
This chapter focuses on how you can monitor, manage, and administer your workloads in an
efficient and proactive manner. To host your applications in the cloud, you need to design end-
to-end infrastructure resources that fulfill the core requirements of compute, networking,
storage, and database services, while also incorporating security best practices and cost
optimization.
To manage your workloads effectively, you must monitor and observe the health of your
resources, ensuring high performance and reliability while mitigating potential bottlenecks.
Here, Amazon CloudWatch offers a suite of features to help you monitor your workloads,
identify resource utilization, and perform extensive observability tasks required to ensure you
consistently deliver optimal performance.
Security, along with the ability to audit access, is critically important to prevent unauthorized
access and minimize attack surfaces. Using AWS CloudTrail, you can audit management and
data access patterns, providing visibility into potential malicious activities within your AWS
accounts.
In addition, tracking changes to resource configurations plays a vital role in cloud operations.
You want to avoid misaligned configuration changes and ensure that all changes and resource
configurations remain compliant with industry-standard best practices and corporate
governance requirements. AWS Config helps you manage change control across your cloud
workloads
This chapter also introduced AWS Systems Manager, a suite of tools designed to help you
efficiently administer your resources in a secure and automated manner.
Together, these tools and services play a critical role in ensuring the smooth operation of the
underlying infrastructure that supports your application requirements and overall customer
experience.
In this chapter, you learned how to monitor, audit, manage, and govern AWS resources using
services such as Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Config, AWS Systems Manager,
and AWS Trusted Advisor. In the next chapter, you will build on that operational foundation by
focusing on security: understanding the Shared Responsibility Model, meeting compliance
requirements, securing data and applications, and using AWS tools such as WAF, Shield,
Inspector, Macie, GuardDuty, and Detective to protect cloud workloads.

Security Fundamentals and Tools
on AWS
Over the last few years, you may have heard about several high-profile security breaches and
data leaks involving household brand names in the news. Cyber-attacks of all kinds have been
on the rise, and given the advancement in technology, you would be forgiven for thinking that
such security issues would decrease.
On the contrary, popular online applications offering email services, trading platforms, and
storage services have had to enforce stricter security protocols to protect user accounts. These
include idx_c35debec mandatory multi-factor authentication (MFA) and idx_f15fdf31 stricter Know Your Customer
(KYC) documentation requirements. These measures have become necessary in recent years.
In this chapter, you will learn about the importance of designing, deploying, and managing
your applications and idx_c6e03894 resources using a zero-trust approach. You will explore the
fundamentals of the Shared Responsibility Model between the cloud provider and the
customer, understand the need for regulatory compliance, and discover the various AWS tools
and services that can help you efficiently secure your workloads.
As you architect and build solutions, you must integrate security measures and protocols in
accordance with best practices at every layer — from the physical infrastructure where
resources reside, such as cloud provider data centers, through the network and transport
layers, all the way up to the application layer. Each layer must be protected.
The following topics are covered in this chapter:
Applying the Shared Responsibility Model
Meeting compliance requirements with AWS programs
Testing workload security with AWS vulnerability scanning
Securing data with AWS encryption services
Protecting web applications with AWS WAF
Mitigating DDoS attacks with AWS Shield
Identifying vulnerabilities with Amazon Inspector
Discovering, detecting, and investigating threats with Amazon Macie, GuardDuty, and
Detective
Applying the Shared Responsibility Model
With on-premises idx_28777c6b networks and data centers, you are solely responsible for the security you
architect and implement for your applications — from the physical security that determines
who can enter data center facilities and server rooms, through to how the application is made
accessible over the Internet and other external networks.
With cloud providers, however, the responsibility for designing and implementing the same

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 16 472
chunks.content:
high level of security best practices does not fall on the provider alone. Instead, it is shared
between the customer and the cloud service provider.
You can rest assured that AWS designs and enforces physical security measures to ensure that
only authorized personnel are granted access to the underlying infrastructure hosting your
cloud resources and applications. AWS implements security controls to protect the physical
network, underlying firewall services, and all security layers up to the hypervisor that runs
your compute resources.
With managed services such as Amazon RDS and DynamoDB, additional security protocols are
followed — for example, ensuring that the infrastructure supporting these services is regularly
patched with critical security updates.
However, as a customer, you are responsible for securing how you build and deploy your
applications in the cloud. You must ensure that your data is encrypted using the security tools
provided by AWS. This is where the concept of the Shared Responsibility Model comes in. The
diagram in Figure 17.1 illustrates idx_38ff0902 how the Shared Responsibility Model is structured:

AWS is responsible for the security of the cloud. This includes enforcing strict security
protocols across the global infrastructure — its data centers (located across Regions and
Availability Zones), edge locations, content delivery infrastructure, storage systems,
networking components, and the hypervisors that support compute services.
As a customer, you are responsible for security in the cloud. This includes:
Implementing strong IAM policies
Enforcing MFA
Securing applications with authentication and authorization controls
Encrypting data
Patching EC2 instances to address vulnerabilities
Protecting data stored in services such as Amazon S3
Ultimately, if you can configure a resource, for example, an Amazon S3 bucket used to host your
data, then how that idx_191a74ea resource is configured is your responsibility.
In the next section, you will learn about how AWS ensures compliance with regulatory
requirements.

477 Security Fundamentals and Tools on AWS
Meeting compliance requirements with AWS
programs
AWS offers compliance idx_7bb1165a programs aligned with a idx_32278b54 wide range of global regulatory and legal
standards. Depending on the nature of your business, you may need to ensure that any
applications or workloads hosted on AWS meet specific compliance requirements. To that end,
you can verify whether AWS participates in the necessary compliance programs.
For example, if you plan to process and store credit card information, your application must
meet the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS). At the same time, AWS
must ensure idx_3ad67a7e that the underlying infrastructure used to host the application is also aligned with
these requirements.
Similarly, if you are a healthcare organization based in the United States, you must comply
with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) of 1996. This means
your application idx_3fed22df must be designed to be HIPAA-compliant. Any patient information stored
must be secured, confidential, and encrypted. Access idx_92cab3ab to patient Protected Health Information
(PHI) must be granted only to authorized personnel.
While there is no formal HIPAA idx_d8e12935 certification for a cloud service provider (CSP) such as AWS,
AWS aligns with HIPAA's risk management expectations through frameworks such as
FedRAMP and NIST 800-53. These are higher security standards that map to the HIPAA
Security Rule and support compliance.
In addition to its wide range of compliance idx_692d92f3 programs, AWS also offers AWS Artifact — a self-
service portal that provides on-demand access to security and compliance reports (such as ISO,
SOC, and PCI) as well as idx_05f711c3 agreements idx_d4751e38 like the Business Associate Addendum (BAA) and Non-

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 17 476
chunks.content:
Disclosure Agreements (NDAs).
When it comes to security, prevention is always better than a cure. As a business, you must be
able to demonstrate that your resources and application workloads are well secured and
resilient against idx_dd8747b0 potential threats. One idx_d3c46856 way to assess your security posture is to run simulated
tests to evaluate how penetrable your environment may be.
In the next section, you will learn more about AWS Vulnerability Scanning options.
Securing data with AWS encryption services
As an AWS customer, you must ensure that the workloads and applications you deploy are
highly secure idx_ccba8780 and accessible only to authorized idx_4071c6df entities. However, unless you actively test your
security posture, you cannot be certain that your configurations and architecture align with
your security requirements.

AWS allows you to run specific types of scans against your own cloud workloads to identify
potential vulnerabilities. Also idx_1c3ea55e known as penetration testing, this involves simulating cyber-
attacks against your computing resources to uncover weaknesses. These activities should be
carried out by internal or authorized security teams.
That said, not all types of scans and simulated attacks are permitted. For instance, you are
prohibited from using tools to idx_f25c04af perform Denial of Service (DoS) testing. Simulated
Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks may only idx_d46c7ad8 be conducted idx_4917fc7a by an AWS Partner
Network (APN) partner that has been pre-approved by AWS to perform such testing.

scans against, as well as certain types of simulations that are prohibited.

Ensure that the tests you run are against your own workloads. As a customer, you are not
permitted to conduct any security assessments of AWS infrastructure or the AWS services
themselves.
These prohibited activities apply across AWS security assessments and are not always
specific to a single service. Always review the latest AWS Customer Support Policy for

Tip
479 Security Fundamentals and Tools on AWS
In Chapter 6, you were introduced to Amazon S3 encryption, which focused on how you can
encrypt the data you store in your Amazon S3 buckets. However, encryption options can also
be applied to other idx_c18e5563 resource idx_90ef7dd9 types, such as encrypting your EBS volumes or RDS Databases. In
the next section, you will learn more about encryption options on AWS.
Securing data with AWS encryption services
Encryption is the process of making data unreadable to unauthorized users and applications.
Plain text data is scrambled using an encryption key and an algorithm. The only way to get
back the plain text is to have the appropriate decryption key.
There are two types of encryption:
Encryption in transit: This is idx_d2d0096e when data is being transmitted across networks, such as
when you access a website using a browser
Encryption at rest: This is when data is being stored on a storage medium, such as a

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 17 478
chunks.content:
hard drive
AWS offers services to help you design and implement encryption for data both in transit and
at rest.
For data in transit, you must idx_f20d6e55 transmit the data using Secure Sockets Layer/Transport Layer
Security (SSL/TLS). This idx_dca472cd requires the sending and receiving nodes to establish a secure
connection, such as the HTTPS protocol. To establish the encrypted connection, you must use
X.509 certificates that you can either purchase from a third-party certificate authority or idx_7913925f create
using the AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) service.
To protect data at rest, you must create an encryption key to encrypt and decrypt data as it is
stored and retrieved from a given storage medium, such as an Amazon EBS volume or an EFS
file store. Encryption and decryption keys are data files containing a long series of numbers
and/or letters that are used by a cryptographic algorithm to encode and decode data. Examples
of algorithms you idx_d5debcfa may idx_eeb08fad have heard idx_392c5fff of include Triple DES or Advanced Encryption Standard
(AES-256) encryption.
An encryption key can be either symmetric or asymmetric:
Symmetric keys use the same key idx_bd8362fe for both encrypting and decrypting the data.
Asymmetric keys are a combination idx_ce04b15f of a public/private key pair. You use the public
key to encrypt the data, and only someone who has access to the private key of that
pair can decrypt it.
In an on-premises environment, you may need to procure the necessary infrastructure to create
and manage encryption and decryption keys, as well as perform the actual task of encrypting
•
•
•
•

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 17 480
chunks.content:
Chapter 17 480
and decrypting data idx_b498ea10 yourself. However, AWS offers its Key Management Service (KMS),
which takes away much of the underlying heavy lifting from you.
With KMS, you can create and idx_e1d4e554 manage customer-managed keys (CMKs), which are used in
conjunction with AWS services that integrate with KMS to encrypt the data those services store
on your behalf. Using customer-managed keys gives you a higher level of control over the
lifecycle and usage of your keys.
AWS also provides AWS-managed keys, which are created and managed automatically by
AWS on behalf of a idx_24eb4c09 service (for example, aws/ebs or aws/rds). These keys are free to use but
offer limited control compared to customer-managed keys and are commonly used as the
default encryption option for many AWS services.
You can also use AWS-owned keys if you do not want the overhead of managing keys or
paying for customer-managed idx_98ba90e8 keys. AWS-owned keys are fully managed by AWS and are used
automatically by some services behind the scenes. You can use these keys to encrypt and
decrypt your data, but you do not have control over the lifecycle of the key, and you do not see
them in your account. You are also not charged for using these keys.
The AWS Key Management Service (KMS) uses shared idx_9ece96c4 hardware security modules to
generate the necessary key material that is then used to create your encryption keys. Although
this is highly secure and uses Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS 140-2)
validated idx_5d23103e hardware, it is nevertheless shared with other customers, which means you do not
have complete control over the hardware security modules. In some cases, this might be
unacceptable idx_ce4a8953 depending idx_32ea1f6b on the industry your business operates in.
In the next section, you will learn more about how you can use your own hardware security
modules in the cloud to create and manage your keys.
AWS CloudHSM
AWS CloudHSM is a dedicated idx_c32aacb3 hardware security module (HSM) that allows you to generate
and manage your encryption keys for use with AWS services to encrypt and decrypt your data.
These hardware modules are placed in your VPC and managed by AWS. While AWS takes care
of provisioning these hardware modules, you are fully responsible for generating, storing,
importing, and exporting your cryptographic keys. AWS does not have access to your keys and
cannot recover them if you lose those keys. It is recommended that you have at least a
minimum of two CloudHSM devices for failover and to avoid a single point of failure. This
obviously increases the cost, but it is highly advised.
AWS CloudHSM complies with FIPS 140-3 (Level 3) and is ideal when AWS KMS is not enough
from a control, compliance, and trust perspective. For example, a government organization

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 17 480
chunks.content:
may prefer to have its own CloudHSM devices rather than use KMS.
481 Security Fundamentals and Tools on AWS
Protecting your data using encryption technologies is fundamental to enforcing your security
posture. However, you must also ensure that your applications are secured and protected from
malicious idx_889789b1 attacks. In the next section, you will learn about an AWS service designed to protect
your application from common web exploits and attacks.
Protecting web applications with AWS WAF
AWS Web Application Firewall (WAF) is designed to offer firewall protection at the
application layer, protecting idx_f7497a7e your idx_846e04cf workloads over standard HTTP and HTTPS protocols. The
service integrates with various application layer entry points published through Amazon
CloudFront, Amazon API Gateway REST APIs, and Application Load Balancers.
This allows you to protect your applications against common web exploits such as cross-site
scripting and SQL injection attacks. With AWS WAF, you create web access control lists (web
ACLs), define rules that fall within specific criteria, and specify the actions to take if any web
request matches that criterion, such as dropping requests suspected to be malicious.
Next, you will learn about another security tool that helps prevent network attacks.
Mitigating DDoS attacks with AWS Shield
AWS Shield offers idx_3a7c468c protection idx_fa6bac8b against Distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks. This is an
attack type where bad actors attempt to overwhelm your applications, networks, and resources
by sending a flood of internet traffic. Your resources cannot cope with the load and end up
denying access to authorized users, resulting in customer dissatisfaction, reputational damage,
and ultimately financial loss.
AWS offers two tiers for the AWS Shield service. These are:
AWS Shield Standard: This is offered idx_08515ead free of cost for AWS customers and protects
against common network and transport layer DDoS attacks on your websites and
applications. AWS Shield Standard can be used with Amazon CloudFront and Route 53
to provide layered protection against known infrastructure attacks. This means that to
benefit from the standard offering, your architecture must make use of these services.
AWS Shield Advanced: This tier offers additional protection against attacks on your
EC2 instances, load balancers, CloudFront distributions, Global Accelerator, and more.
The service offers real-time detection, proactive monitoring, and automatic mitigation
of application layer (Layer 7) attacks. In addition, when you subscribe to the advanced
version, you get access to the AWS Shield Response Team (SRT), an expert idx_fbd53e2a team
available 24/7 for manual intervention and support. AWS also reimburses costs for
scaling resources, such as auto-scaling your EC2 instances due to DDoS attacks.

cost of $3,000 per month.
In the next section, you will learn how to protect your EC2 instances from unintended network
access and manage operating system vulnerabilities through effective patch and update
monitoring.
Identifying vulnerabilities with Amazon Inspector
AWS offers a wide idx_37d0b021 range of tools to protect your network, infrastructure resources as well as
your applications from malicious attacks. However, prevention is always better than cure, and
one such service that you must add to your toolkit is AWS Inspector. This service continuously
assesses the network exposure and software vulnerabilities of your EC2, Lambda functions,
and code scans, as well as container workloads.
With AWS Inspector, you can detect open ports and identify whether the operating system or
applications running on your instances are known to have vulnerabilities that need to be
patched.
AWS Inspector integrates with AWS Systems Manager to collect telemetry data from your
instances. The service automatically scans your workloads and compares findings against
security intelligence idx_fd1a6736 sources such as the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE)
database.
AWS Inspector evaluates:
Network exposure: Identifying instances that may be reachable from the internet
Software vulnerabilities: Detecting known vulnerabilities in operating systems and
installed applications
The findings are idx_f9b54907 presented in the AWS Inspector dashboard with granular data to help you
identify potential vulnerabilities. You can then take necessary action to resolve these.
While analyzing your EC2 instances, Lambda code, and containers to detect vulnerabilities is
crucial, you must also ensure that your data is protected from unauthorized access.
Specifically, you must ensure that idx_09ca2563 you protect personally identifiable information (PII) and
track how it is being used, enforcing guardrails to prevent unauthorized access.
This is where services such as Amazon Macie, GuardDuty, and Detective become useful, as they
help you identify sensitive data, detect suspicious activity, and investigate potential security
issues across your AWS environment.

483 Security Fundamentals and Tools on AWS
Discovering, detecting, and investigating threats with
Amazon Macie, GuardDuty, and Detective
The following services approach security from different but complementary angles. Amazon
Macie focuses on discovering and protecting sensitive data, GuardDuty helps detect potential
threats and malicious activity, and Detective supports deeper investigation when you need to

chunks.heading: Chapter 17 482
chunks.content:
understand the root cause of a security finding.
Amazon Macie
Amazon Macie is a fully managed idx_a1c59651 data security and privacy service designed to help protect
Personally Identifiable Information (PII) and Protected Health Information (PHI) stored idx_88842503
in your idx_5adc89f9 Amazon S3 buckets.
Amazon Macie uses machine learning and pattern-matching capabilities to discover sensitive
data and track changes to your buckets by identifying new or modified objects over time. The
service can be used to perform on-demand analysis or run automated data discovery jobs,
reporting its findings through dashboards and alerts.
Amazon Macie can also be used in a multi-account architecture by monitoring your buckets
across multiple accounts within an AWS Organizations configuration. This means you can
designate a single Macie administrator account to centrally manage and help prevent data
leaks across all member accounts.
In the next section, you will learn about another service designed to detect malicious activity
against your AWS account.
AWS GuardDuty
AWS GuardDuty is idx_ec0c9508 a threat detection service designed to help you identify potential malicious
activity against your AWS accounts and applications.
The service uses various threat intelligence feeds, such as known malicious IP addresses and
domains, and applies machine learning to analyze data from Amazon CloudTrail event logs,
VPC Flow Logs, and Route 53 DNS logs.
AWS GuardDuty can detect the use of compromised credentials, communication with
malicious IP addresses, as well as unusual activity carried out in your AWS account based on
past behavior — for example, if a fleet of EC2 instances is launched in a region you do not
normally operate in, or if Amazon S3 API calls originate from an unexpected remote host, or if
unauthorized access attempts are made from known malicious IP addresses.

AWS GuardDuty provides detailed findings in the GuardDuty console, integrates with Amazon
EventBridge and AWS Security Hub, and makes it easier to identify potential malicious activity
that you can act on to better protect your environment.
Next, you will learn idx_fb732835 about another AWS service designed to help identify the root cause of
potential security issues.
Amazon Detective
So far, you have learned idx_0d5e581c about various security tools that can help you detect data leaks,
potential malicious activity, and even protect against DDoS attacks. In addition, you have
access to logging and monitoring data from tools such as Amazon CloudWatch and AWS
CloudTrail. If you need to analyze all this data and identify the root cause of security issues,
you will traditionally have to extract these individual data sources and build an Extract,
Transform, and Load (ETL) solution to idx_74f26d1f perform a deep-dive analysis.
AWS offers Amazon Detective, designed to help you perform root cause analysis of your
security issues without the need to build complex ETL processes. The service automatically
collects and analyzes time-based events such as login activity and network traffic from AWS
CloudTrail and VPC Flow Logs, and ingests findings from AWS GuardDuty to build
visualizations and identify behaviors over time.
Ultimately, Amazon Detective helps you perform a deeper analysis of your security data and
identify the root cause of security breaches and malicious activity.
In the next section, you will have the opportunity to configure Amazon Macie to analyze raw
data held in an Amazon idx_771ee7fd S3 bucket and identify potential PII that must be protected.
Project task 17 – Preventing employee data leaks at
Belly Brew Co. Limited
The HR team at Belly Brew Co. Limited idx_4438516b has been extremely idx_37d555d1 busy over the past week preparing
for a new Point of Sales training program across various cafes in the UK. They recently
uploaded employee records documents to a folder in Amazon S3 to support internal workforce
analysis. However, the data was mistakenly uploaded to the wrong S3 bucket.
Although the bucket belonged to HR, it was intended for storing only training materials — not
employee personal records. As a result, sensitive information such as employee contract
details, dates of birth, and National Insurance numbers was stored in an inappropriate
location.

Amazon Macie can be configured to analyze the contents of these buckets and identify the
presence idx_5b175714 of any Personally Identifiable Information (PII).
Organizations can quickly detect such issues and take appropriate action. In this case, the issue
was not permissions-driven because HR had access to multiple buckets and happened to
